episodes.title: What will computer chips look like in 2045?
episodes.about: Dwarkesh spent two days touring Intel's most advanced fab and talking to its technical leadership about what the chips of the future will look like: gate-all-around transistors, backside power, CFET, and hybrid bonding. He also asks Intel's leadership how the semiconductor industry will cope with the enormous demand shock from AI. AI compute has grown 3x a year for the last decade, but according to Intel's CTO, Intel could only double leading-edge wafer production with today's global stock of chipmaking tools.
episodes.why: Always-include show, out yesterday: a two-day tour of Intel's most advanced fab, and the CTO on what happens when AI compute demand grows 3x a year but wafer output can only double.

episodes.title: The AI vs AI Battle for the Internet
episodes.about: AI attackers and AI defenders are now battling over the internet's vulnerabilities at superhuman speed. A massive PHP exploit and a wave of attacks reveal why cybersecurity is entering a new era - and why businesses are struggling to keep up. In the headlines: Anthropic unveils Claude Duet, Walmart welcomes shopping agents, and Meta turns to new stock to fund its AI buildout.
episodes.why: Attackers and defenders are fighting over a massive PHP exploit at machine speed; headlines include Anthropic's new Claude Duet and Walmart opening the door to shopping agents.

episodes.title: Airbnb Is Building a ‘Company Brain’ for AI Agents with Ahmad Al-Dahle - #781
episodes.about: AI agents need the institutional knowledge experienced employees rely on: why a system works a certain way, which policies apply, and what never made it into the documentation. Capturing that knowledge is hard; keeping it useful may be harder. Airbnb CTO Ahmad Al-Dahle shares how his team is building Project Everest, a 'company brain' that captures knowledge from employees' workflows for AI agents. They explore stale information and context poisoning, why too much context can backfire, how the team evaluates whether shared knowledge improves engineering work, and measuring AI productivity beyond token usage and PR counts.
episodes.why: Airbnb's CTO on Project Everest, the company brain feeding agents the undocumented know-how employees carry - and why too much context poisons it.

episodes.title: Can Living Neurons Make AI 5x Faster?
episodes.about: Neurosurgeon-scientists Alex Ksendzovsky and Jon Pomeraniec explain how The Biological Computing Company uses living neurons as a research platform for AI. Their team grows roughly 150,000 cells on a 4,096-electrode array, sends in patterns such as handwritten digits, records how the neurons respond, and models useful computational behaviors in software. They say those neuron-inspired techniques are already helping GPU-based video-generation systems run about 5x faster with roughly 80% lower inference cost, while their longer-term work explores robots, world models, and real-time biological compute.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — The Neuron is a daily AI explainer show new to this list: two neurosurgeon-scientists growing 150,000 living neurons on an electrode array, claiming 5x faster video generation at 80% lower inference cost.

episodes.title: Kazuo Ishiguro on emotional truth in sci-fi and in our AI reality
episodes.about: The movie 'Klara and the Sun,' in theaters now, is based on the 2021 novel of the same name by Kazuo Ishiguro. The story is set in the future and is narrated by Klara, a robotic 'Artificial Friend,' whose job is to be a companion to a sick teenage girl. In the 5 years since the release of the novel, the AI landscape has changed profoundly. Ishiguro talks about the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence, the intersection of art and science, and his hopes - and fears - for the future of this tech.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — Science Friday is the long-running public-radio science show, new to this list: Nobel laureate Kazuo Ishiguro on what 'Klara and the Sun' got right about AI companions, five years and one AI boom later.
